items.claim: A validator that rejects literal CR/LF but anchors with ^...$ without DOTALL still passes a percent-encoded %0d%0a payload that a downstream decoder turns back into a real line terminator.
items.body: The filter rejects the literal bytes (0x0d 0x0a). A second layer — a router, a redirect helper, a framework header writer, or a reverse proxy — percent-decodes the value before it reaches the HTTP serializer. The serializer then sees a real line terminator and emits a header line break. The bypass is therefore a decode-order defect: what the filter sees is not what the serializer sees. Record: plain-value rejection, the bypass variant that passed, and the observed effect at the sink (an injected header line or second header block).
items.disproof: Uniform rejection: literal CRLF, %0d%0a, %0a, %0d and double-encoded %250d%250a all produce the same control response — one header block, no injected header, unchanged body. If the endpoint normalises or rejects after decoding rather than only before, the bypass is closed.

sources.quote: a URL that looks harmless is not, because decoding the percent-encoded characters yields the live payload
unexpected newline characters may be introduced specifically to bypass brittle validation, so normalize or encode input so it represents a single line BEFORE validating

items.claim: Modern language-level header setters defeat naive CRLF payloads without any application sanitiser, because a value containing CR or LF raises a TypeError instead of being serialised, so a payload that is not percent-decoded twice and not split-and-rejoined before reaching the setter cannot inject a header.
items.body: Modern language-level header setters refuse to serialise a header value containing CR or LF, raising a TypeError instead. A payload that is not double-percent-decoded and not split-and-rejoined before reaching the setter therefore cannot inject a header. Treat this as a bypass it is — the concrete observation (a controlled request/response pair) must be recorded before any finding is reportable. The rule is wrong when the value is passed through a path that bypasses the guarded setter: a raw socket write, a C library or framework API taking a pre-built header block, a template or config file that emits headers, or a reverse proxy that re-serialises a stored value.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the value reaches the wire through a bypass path — a raw write to the socket, a C library or framework API that takes a pre-built header block, a template or config file that emits headers, or a reverse proxy that re-serialises a stored value — because those paths re-introduce the injection the TypeError was meant to prevent.

items.claim: Response splitting succeeds when attacker bytes are emitted as a new header line inside a response whose Content-Type and framing still let a second header block or injected header be honoured.
items.body: Craft: GET /go?u=x with a parameter that lands in Location, payload x%0d%0aSet-Cookie:%20pwn=1%0d%0a%0d%0a<script>alert(1)</script>. Read the raw response as bytes, not through a client library that normalises headers. A genuine split shows TWO header blocks: the original response ends at the injected blank line and a complete second response follows, or at minimum an injected header line appears before the real blank line. Record which framing mode (identity, gzip, chunked) the split reproduces in — a split that only reproduces with Content-Encoding: gzip is still a split.
items.disproof: If the raw response contains exactly one header block, ends at a single blank line, contains no injected header, and has a body identical to the control request's body, response splitting did not occur. Repeat for the raw-CRLF, %0d%0a, chunked and gzip variants; if all four come back structurally identical, the claim is false.

sources.quote: a request URL in which every CRLF is percent-encoded, %0D%0A, threading an injected </textarea>, an injected <form action="/logout"> and a hidden authenticity_token field between them
the injector only proceeds when the response Content-Type and the attacker-specified Content-Type match, and it handles both chunked Transfer-Encoding and gzip Content-Encoding

items.claim: A CRLF finding is validated by showing that a line terminator survives into the emitted response, and that the response's body framing (identity, chunked, gzip) does not neutralise the injected boundary.
items.body: Two-part validation. Part one, survival: replay the payload and assert on raw bytes that a second header line or a second header block exists; assert on the bytes, not on a client library that raises on a malformed response. Part two, framing: re-run the same payload with Accept-Encoding: gzip and separately with a chunked request, and inspect the decoded body. A finding that only reproduces in one framing mode is still a finding — record which mode, because that tells the defender where the fix belongs.
items.disproof: A raw response in which the line terminator never appears: one header block, one blank line, no injected header, and a body whose decoded content equals the control response's decoded body. If that holds across identity, gzip and chunked framings for both the literal-CRLF and %0d%0a payloads, the CRLF did not survive.

items.claim: The signal for CRLF is a differential: a raw CR/LF and its percent-encoded %0d%0a form produce different header structure, and only one of them is rejected.
items.body: Send the same logical payload three ways to the same parameter and diff the RAW response: (1) literal CRLF via curl --data-binary with actual 0x0d 0x0a, (2) %0d%0a percent-encoded, (3) a single encoded %0a and separately %0d. Interpret: if (2) yields an extra header or a truncated body while (1) is rejected, the filter sees the literal control characters but not the encoded form — the classic bypass. If both are neutralised the endpoint is filtering. If (1) splits and (2) does not, the filter is decoding.
items.disproof: A single request with %0d%0aX-Injected: yes returns exactly one header block, no X-Injected, and the same body as the control request with x in that position, across raw CRLF, %0d%0a, %0a and %0d.

items.claim: Seeing a %0d%0a payload echoed back in an HTML error page or response body is not CRLF injection: the flaw requires the injected CR and LF to become additional header field lines in the response, which the server's HTTP serializer, not the template engine, controls.
items.body: The reflected value is the first observable step only if it is later re-emitted through a header-emitting API — stored and replayed by a Location or Set-Cookie header, or re-serialised by a downstream proxy/CDN into a response header. Record the byte position of the payload relative to the header/body boundary before classifying anything. This looks like CRLF injection (a %0d%0a payload comes back verbatim) but is actually inert text in an HTML body, separated by the bytes landing after the header/body boundary rather than inside a header value.
items.disproof: Disproof is positional and byte-exact: the injected string occurs only after the single blank line that terminates the header block, the response has exactly one header block, no Set-Cookie (or other injected header) appears in the header block, and a cookie jar from a real client run shows no new cookie. If all four hold, the payload was reflected as body text and this is not CRLF injection.

items.claim: A CRLF defect in a response emitted onto a REUSED connection chains into injecting headers and a URL into a SUBSEQUENT, unrelated request, so the victim of the injected header is not the attacker.
items.body: A CRLF defect in a response emitted onto a REUSED connection chains into injecting headers and a URL into a SUBSEQUENT, unrelated request, so the victim of the injected header is not the attacker — the second request is a separate entity that receives data the origin never saw. Test with a pipelined two-request sequence in which request 2 arrives at the origin with only its own headers and its own URL. Confirm the chain by observing the injected header/URL on the subsequent request at the origin, not merely on the first response.
items.disproof: Disproof is any one of: the connection is not reused (each response carries Connection: close, so there is no second request to poison); the injected header does not appear on the subsequent request as observed at the origin; or the framing mismatch is corrected before the response is emitted, so request 2 is parsed cleanly. A pipelined two-request test in which request 2 arrives at the origin with only its own headers and its own URL disproves the chain.
